bib.title: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation", Patrice Béchard and Orlando Marquez Ayala (ServiceNow), arXiv:2404.08189v1 [cs.LG], 12 Apr 2024. The Acknowledgements thank the NAACL reviewers, so it is likely an industry-track paper. The text says no venue.
COVERAGE: 40,402 of 40,402 chars read, including the appendices (training details, Tables 6 and 7, error examples). The Figure 4 text is truncated in the extraction. Figure 1-4 content is image-only. Nothing else was skipped.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Adding a fine-tuned retriever that suggests step and table names cuts hallucinated steps and tables sharply in a fine-tuned StarCoderBase workflow generator.
  number: hallucinated steps about 0.14-0.16 without a retriever, 0.017-0.072 with one. Hallucinated tables about 0.19-0.21 without, 0.016-0.044 with.
  setup: Human Eval split (157 examples). Fine-tuned StarCoderBase at 1B, 3B, 7B and 15.5B. JSON workflow generation (IT domain). Greedy decoding. Single run, no variance reported.
  quote: "without a retriever (only LLM fine-tuning), the % of hallucinated steps and tables can be as high as 21% on the "Human Eval" split. Using a retriever, this decreases to less than 7.5% for steps and less than 4.5% for tables with all StarCoderBase LLMs."
  where: Sec 5.2, p6, Table 4
- Claim: A 3B model with RAG matches a 15.5B model without RAG on Trigger EM and Bag of Steps, with low hallucination. RAG therefore lets a smaller LLM be deployed.
  number: 3B+RAG: Trigger EM 0.615, BofS 0.641, HS 0.017, HT 0.030. 15.5B without RAG: 0.632, 0.662, 0.160, 0.194.
  setup: Human Eval, as above. The 3B and 15.5B models are the same family. The 7B+RAG model has Trigger EM 0.664, BofS 0.672 and is chosen as the best trade-off. 15.5B+RAG scores 0.667 and 0.667.
  quote: "the 3B version trained with RAG is competitive even with the 15.5B version without RAG on the Trigger EM and Bag of Steps metrics, while keeping hallucination low."
  where: Sec 5.2, p6, Table 4
- Claim: Fine-tuning the retriever matters far more than scaling an off-the-shelf encoder.
  number: Step Recall@15 and Table Recall@10. gtr-t5-base (110M) 0.505/0.489. gtr-t5-xxl (4.8B) 0.561/0.489. all-mpnet-base-v2 (110M) untuned 0.425/0.170. Fine-tuned with all negative strategies 0.743/0.766.
  setup: Human Eval. The fine-tuned encoder is all-mpnet-base-v2 (110M), trained on about 15,000 step pairs and 1,500 table pairs. Negative strategies: random 0.640/0.752, BM25 0.537/0.586, ANCE 0.556/0.699.
  quote: "Scaling the size of the off-the-shelf encoders, as we did with GTR-T5, does not yield significant improvements on both retrieval metrics." "What was crucial to significantly improve the performance was fine-tuning the encoder."
  where: Sec 5.1, p5, Table 3
- Claim: Combining random, BM25 and ANCE negatives beats any single strategy. Step recall rises from 0.640 (random) to 0.743 (all). Table recall rises from 0.752 to 0.766.
  number: 0.743 / 0.766
  setup: Table 3, Human Eval, contrastive loss on query-JSON object pairs.
  quote: "+ All 0.743 0.766"
  where: Table 3, p5
- Claim: With the retriever, out-of-domain performance roughly matches in-domain performance, without retuning the retriever or the LLM. Removing the suggestions at inference raises hallucinated tables from 0.066 to 0.428.
  number: OOD weighted avg with RAG: Trigger EM 0.647, BofS 0.714, HS 0.018, HT 0.066. No-RAG avg: 0.544, 0.629, 0.020, 0.428. Human Eval: 0.664, 0.672, 0.019, 0.042.
  setup: RAG fine-tuned StarCoderBase-7B on five OOD splits (42 to 429 examples each) from other deployments (HR, finance and others). 7% to 76% of steps are not in Train. The "No RAG" row is the same RAG-trained model run with the suggestions removed, not a model trained without RAG.
  quote: "We observe that on average, thanks to the retriever, all the OOD metrics are similar to the in-domain results represented by the "Human Eval" split."
  where: Sec 5.3, p6, Table 5
- Claim: Without suggestions the RAG-trained model hallucinates about the same share of steps. It becomes conservative and reuses steps seen in training. It invents tables much more often.
  number: HS 0.020 without suggestions vs 0.018 with. HT 0.428 vs 0.066.
  setup: Same as the previous claim. This is the authors' inspection of outputs, not a controlled test.
  quote: "the RAG fine-tuned model has learned to be conservative in generating steps when it does not receive suggestions, relying only on steps that it has seen during training."
  where: Sec 5.3, p6
- Claim: Hallucination by unique name is higher than the per-workflow rate. Suggestions cut the unique hallucinated step rate on OOD1 from 40% to 13%, but some splits stay above 10%.
  number: OOD1 unique step names 52 with 40% hallucinated without suggestions, 100 with 13% hallucinated with suggestions. OOD3 37% to 9%. OOD5 17% to 3%. OOD4 rises from 5% to 9%. Unique hallucinated table names with suggestions: 9% to 22%.
  setup: Tables 6 and 7, RAG fine-tuned StarCoderBase-7B on the OOD splits.
  quote: "even with suggestions, there is still an important gap in the percentage of unique step names that are hallucinated, as in some splits more than 10% of unique steps are invented."
  where: Appendix B, p10
- Claim: Larger LLMs copy retrieved items better, so scaling gives more consistent gains under RAG. The 1B RAG model hallucinates much more than 3B and larger.
  number: HS with RAG: 1B 0.072, 3B 0.017, 7B 0.019, 15.5B 0.040.
  setup: Table 4, Human Eval.
  quote: "This suggests that larger LLMs can better copy and paste retrieved steps and tables during generation."
  where: Sec 5.2, p6
- Claim: Code-pretrained StarCoderBase-7B outperformed CodeLlama-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.1 when all were fine-tuned with RAG. The authors only suspect why.
  number: Trigger EM 0.664 vs 0.623 and 0.596. BofS 0.672 vs 0.617 and 0.617.
  setup: Table 4, same data and hyperparameters.
  quote: "We suspect that pre-training on large amounts of natural language data may be detrimental to our task."
  where: Sec 5.2, p6
- Claim: Training design. The retriever and LLM are trained separately. The LLM is trained as if retrieval recall were 100%. The most frequent steps are left out of the suggestions. Retrieved JSON objects are put in the prompt before the user query so the LLM can copy them.
  number: none
  setup: Separate retriever and LLM training, in contrast to end-to-end RAG (Lewis et al., 2020). Retrieval uses a FAISS index with cosine similarity over top-K. Decoding is greedy.
  quote: "in every LLM training example, we assume the retriever has 100% recall: the steps and table required to build the structured output are always in the suggestions, except for the most frequent steps."
  where: Sec 3.2, p4
- Claim: Engineering. The 110M retriever shares one GPU with the 7B LLM with negligible effect and could run on CPU. A 7B model allows larger batches, at some latency cost. The decoupled retriever can be reused.
  number: 110M retriever, 7B LLM
  setup: Production deployment. The authors' stress tests and user research found response time "acceptable", with no latency numbers given.
  quote: "allowed us to deploy it on the same GPU with neg-ligible effect on the larger LLM. But we could even deploy the retriever on CPU due to its small size."
  where: Sec 5.5, p7
- Claim: Error analysis. Retrieval misses on rarely used steps cause lower-quality workflows. Logic steps (IF, TRY, FOREACH) are the LLM's typical structural failures.
  number: none
  setup: Qualitative, with examples in Fig 4. Suggested fixes: decompose the query into several retrieval calls, and generate synthetic data for the missed steps.
  quote: "if a crucial component is not in the retriever's suggestions, it becomes difficult for the LLM to generate a valid workflow in line with the user query."
  where: Sec 5.4, p7

LIMITS
- Single task: JSON workflow generation at ServiceNow. The datasets are proprietary and internal, and mostly IT domain.
- Very small eval sets: Human Eval has 157 examples, and the OOD splits have 42 to 429. There are no confidence intervals or seeds. Differences such as 0.017 vs 0.019 are likely noise.
- Retrieves JSON objects (step and table names), not facts or text passages. It does not test classic open-domain QA RAG, so transfer to prose RAG is untested.
- There is no ablation against guided/grammar-constrained decoding. The paper only mentions it as complementary. It does not compare against long-context prompting or in-context stuffing, which the authors call impractical.
- No joint retriever-LLM training was tried (future work). Retrieval recall is only 0.743 for steps, yet the LLM was trained assuming 100% recall.
- The "No RAG Avg" row is the RAG-trained model with suggestions removed, not a model trained without RAG. The no-retriever fine-tuned baselines appear only in Table 4.
- The ethical note concedes that hallucination is not eliminated. Post-processing flags nonexistent steps for users.
- Dated: models are StarCoderBase, CodeLlama-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.1 (2023-era). Paper from 2024.

BUILDS ON: Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG). Gao et al. 2024 (RAG survey). Reimers and Gurevych 2019 (Sentence-BERT, siamese encoder with mean pooling). Li et al. 2023b (SANTA, structure-aware dense retrieval). Xiong et al. 2020 (ANCE negatives). Hadsell et al. 2006 (contrastive loss). Douze et al. 2024 (FAISS). Li et al. 2023a (StarCoder). Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA). Willard and Louf 2023 (guided generation, cited as complementary). Neelakantan et al. 2022 (scaling encoders gives no gain on code retrieval). Shuster et al. 2021 (retrieval reduces hallucination in conversation).

CODE: Equations, verbatim. Retriever: "R(q) =Norm(MeanPool(Enc(q)))" (Eq 2, p3). Loss: "L = 12 Y D2 + (1− Y ) · max(0, 12 − D)2" with "D = 1 − cossim(vq, vs)" (Eq 3, p3-4). The extraction garbles the fractions, which should be 1/2. Hyperparameters (App A, p10). LLM: AdamW, lr 5e-4, 5,000 steps, cosine schedule with 100 warmup, effective batch 32, LoRA r=16, alpha=16, dropout 0.05, single A100 80GB. Retriever: AdamW, lr 2e-5, batch 128, 10 epochs, SentenceTransformers.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): sample JSON workflow output for a natural-language requirement.
- Fig 2 (p3): architecture. The user query goes to both the retriever and the LLM, and the retriever's suggestions are appended to the prompt. The quickest way to see the pipeline.
- Fig 3 (p4): training example. Suggested tables and steps are placed before the user query, and the last four lines are the expected output.
- Fig 4 (p11): perfect output, retrieval error (send_slack_message not suggested), and LLM error (ignored "Try"). Its text is truncated in the extraction.

PROBLEMS: The extraction mangles the Eq 3 fractions and Figure 4 text (truncated). The figures themselves are images and were not viewed. No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. Table 4's bold markers are not preserved, so "best" cells are not identifiable from the text.
